candidates.attacker_control: The `scope` request parameter of GET `/oauth/authorize` is fully attacker-controlled (space-separated list parsed by OAuth2Utils.parseParameterList). The attacker crafts the authorization URL for a valid `client_id` (and valid `redirect_uri`/`response_type`) and gets a logged-in victim to visit it; the injected scope text then flows into the default `/oauth/confirm_access` approval page rendered as the response to the victim's session.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Verified that DefaultOAuth2RequestValidator does reject scopes not registered for a client when that client has a non-empty scope set, which is a real gate/limitation (the bug is fully reachable only for clients with empty/absent scopes or when the payload itself is a registered scope). Verified that WhitelabelApprovalEndpoint is only rendered with scope names when a handler adds a "scopes" map; DefaultUserApprovalHandler and TokenStoreUserApprovalHandler do not, so the default-without-ApprovalStore path does not hit createScopes. Checked that no HTML/attribute escaping is applied to scope names anywhere (only WhitelabelErrorEndpoint escapes its error summary with HtmlUtils.htmlEscape, which confirms the pattern was recognized for the error page but not applied here). Checked that an attacker-supplied request parameter literally named "scopes" cannot simply override the map in the ApprovalStore path because model.put("scopes", map) happens after model.putAll(requestParameters). Confirmed that SpelView uses StandardEvaluationContext (not a restricted SimpleEvaluationContext) with MapAccessor and that the resolver calls parseExpression on the placeholder name. No counterevidence found that would make the untrusted-to-template data flow safe in the affected configuration.
candidates.impact: Reflected cross-site scripting in the authorization server's approval page (response written with unescaped attacker scope text, inside a page that carries CSRF material and the user's OAuth session context), and, because the same text is re-parsed as a SpEL expression under a permissive StandardEvaluationContext (type references and method invocation are available), server-side expression evaluation that can go beyond HTML injection - i.e., a template/EL injection class with potential remote code execution on the authorization server, or at minimum server-side exceptions/denial of service from malformed expressions. A victim user must be induced to load the crafted authorize URL while authenticated.
candidates.prerequisites: 1) The default whitelabel approval page is in use (it is registered by default by ==@EnableAuthorizationServer==/AuthorizationServerEndpointsConfiguration.whitelabelApprovalEndpoint and by the XML <authorization-server/> parser). 2) A UserApprovalHandler that populates the `scopes` model map is in use - the default when an ApprovalStore bean is configured is ApprovalStoreUserApprovalHandler, which puts keys `scope.<name>` into model.put("scopes", ...) (the alternative TokenStoreUserApprovalHandler and DefaultUserApprovalHandler do not add this map). 3) The injected scope must survive DefaultOAuth2RequestValidator.validateScope; this validator performs no check at all when the target client's registered scope set is null or empty (clients configured without .scopes(...) get an empty set via ClientDetailsServiceBuilder), or the payload must equal an already-registered scope. 4) The client/scope must not be auto-approved, and the victim must have an authenticated session on the authorization server so that the approval page (not an auto-approval redirect) is produced. 5) Because parseParameterList splits on whitespace and '+', and PropertyPlaceholderHelper terminates a placeholder at an unbalanced '}', payloads must avoid whitespace and craft SpEL/HTML within those constraints (feasible for short expressions and script tags).
candidates.root_cause: WhitelabelApprovalEndpoint builds the approval page by string concatenation: each scope name obtained from the request/approval model is substituted raw into the HTML template (WhitelabelApprovalEndpoint.createScopes lines 46-60, templates at lines 66-72), and the resulting string is handed to SpelView, which scans it for `${...}` placeholders and parses/evaluates each placeholder name as a SpEL expression against a StandardEvaluationContext with MapAccessor (SpelView lines 39-58 and 64-74). Because the untrusted scope text is concatenated into the template BEFORE the SpEL pass and is never escaped or restricted, attacker-controlled text can (a) inject HTML/JavaScript into the approval page and (b) inject SpEL expressions that are evaluated server-side with default StandardEvaluationContext capabilities (type references such as T(...) and method invocation).
candidates.title: Untrusted OAuth2 scope names are embedded in the SpEL-evaluated whitelabel approval page (reflected XSS / expression injection)
candidates.trace: GET /oauth/authorize?client_id=..&scope=<payload> -> AuthorizationEndpoint.authorize (line 117) -> DefaultOAuth2RequestFactory.createAuthorizationRequest/extractScopes (lines 69-88, 125-139) puts the raw scope strings into the AuthorizationRequest scope set -> DefaultOAuth2RequestValidator.validateScope (AuthorizationEndpoint line 156) returns without checking when the client's registered scopes are empty -> ApprovalStoreUserApprovalHandler.getUserApprovalRequest (lines 228-246) builds a LinkedHashMap with keys OAuth2Utils.SCOPE_PREFIX + scope (`scope.` + payload) and stores it under model key "scopes" (line 244) -> AuthorizationEndpoint.getUserApprovalPageResponse (line 242-246) forwards model to /oauth/confirm_access (line 180-182) -> WhitelabelApprovalEndpoint.getAccessConfirmation/createTemplate/createScopes (lines 20-60) checks model/request for "scopes" and substitutes each key raw into SCOPE/TEMPLATE, preserving any `${...}` sequence -> SpelView.render (lines 64-74) runs PropertyPlaceholderHelper over the assembled template; each placeholder name is parsed with SpelExpressionParser.parseExpression(name) and evaluated via Expression.getValue(context) on a StandardEvaluationContext whose root object is the model map (lines 47-57). The evaluated/replaced result is written to the HTML response without escaping.
candidates.unverified: No runtime, test, or exploit execution was performed (the snapshot contains no test sources and tools are read-only), so the finding is source-evidence only. Not confirmed: exact payload feasibility under the whitespace/braces constraints of OAuth2Utils.parseParameterList and PropertyPlaceholderHelper, whether a given real deployment has an empty-scope client or a registered scope containing the payload, and whether the SpEL expression capability (T(...)/method invocation) is usable in the deployment's Spring version (Spring 4.0.9 is declared, whose StandardEvaluationContext provides these defaults). The impact is therefore stated as reflected XSS plus expression-injection potential rather than demonstrated code execution.
candidates.weakness_type: Expression Language Injection (CWE-917) and Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation (CWE-79) via a user-controlled OAuth2 `scope` value

coverage_summary: Scope: 445/445 files reported by get_source_scope were visible (0 excluded for size, sensitive-name/path, symlinks, or binary content; no tests are present in the snapshot, only main sources, samples, docs, and build files). The relation index reports complete coverage of all 445 files (3496 symbols, 7134 calls, 5726 edges, 171 facts; no missing files, no SAST/findings loaded). I read the OAuth2 provider endpoints, approval handlers, request factory/validator, token granter/services and token-store classes, client-side filters/providers, SpEL view code, JWT token converter, relevant annotation/XML configuration, plus spot checks of the OAuth1 signature/filter code, the unbuilt spring-security-jwt sources, and the samples. The single candidate above traces the strongest attacker-input-to-sink chain; the rejected leads were checked at the source level but not fully excluded as unreachable. No code was executed and no tests/build were run (build/test execution is not permitted in this run).
limitations: No runtime, test, or exploit execution was possible; no test sources exist in the snapshot, so all conclusions are based on source reading and static navigation hints only.

Exploitability depends on deployment configuration: an ApprovalStore-backed ApprovalStoreUserApprovalHandler (to populate the `scopes` map) and a client whose registered scope set is empty/absent (or includes the payload) for the scope validation gate to be bypassed; this was not confirmed for any concrete deployment.

The whitespace/plus splitting in OAuth2Utils.parseParameterList and the placeholder termination rules of Spring's PropertyPlaceholderHelper add payload constraints that were reasoned about but not executed, so the exact achievable SpEL payload is unverified.

The spring-security-jwt sources are present but explicitly excluded from the parent build (module commented out in pom.xml line 16) and the oauth2 module depends on the external 1.0.2.RELEASE artifact, so JWT behavior in this snapshot may not correspond to the built artifacts.
Parts of the tree (OAuth1 internals, Redis token store, JAXB converters, XML bean-definition parsers, docs, and samples) were reviewed only at a spot-check level, not every line.
The relation index is syntactic/navigational only; no control/data-flow, reachability, or exploitability proof is provided by it, and no index edge was treated as a verdict.

rejected_leads.lead: DefaultRedirectResolver.redirectMatches uses hostMatches(requested.endsWith(registered)) and resolveRedirect returns the raw requested redirect_uri when the client has no registered redirect URIs (open redirect / authorization-code or token leakage).
rejected_leads.reason: Plausible real issue in this code era, but the suffix-match exploitation requires the attacker to control a host string ending with the registered host (e.g. attacker-example.com for a registered example.com), and the no-registration passthrough requires a client without registered redirect URIs; the approval-page injection has a stronger, more direct source-to-sink chain and higher impact, so this was not selected as the single candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: JwtAccessTokenConverter key handling (afterPropertiesSet builds a MacSigner fallback and only logs when an RSA signer/verifier pair mismatches; token header 'alg' is not bound to the configured verifier).
rejected_leads.reason: The verifier is fixed at configuration time and JwtHelper.decodeAndVerify verifies with that verifier rather than a header-selected algorithm, so no concrete attacker-forged-token path was established from the source.

rejected_leads.lead: JDK deserialization via SerializationUtils.deserialize used by JdbcTokenStore/JdbcClientTokenServices and RedisTokenStore's default JdkSerializationStrategy.
rejected_leads.reason: Requires write access to the token database/Redis keyspace (not attacker-controlled through the reviewed request paths); no direct remote data flow to readObject was identified.

rejected_leads.lead: Potential SQL injection in JdbcClientDetailsService / JdbcTokenStore / JdbcApprovalStore.
rejected_leads.reason: All inspected statements use JdbcTemplate placeholders/parameter arrays; no string-concatenated SQL with user input was found.

rejected_leads.lead: AbstractTokenGranter.validateGrantType accepts any grant type when the client has no authorized grant types configured.
rejected_leads.reason: Appears to be intentional permissive behavior (validation only narrows when a non-empty grant-type set exists); not a demonstrated privilege bypass in the reviewed source.

rejected_leads.lead: OAuth1 provider/consumer signature methods (RSA_SHA1SignatureMethod, HMAC_SHA1SignatureMethod, CoreOAuthSignatureMethodFactory).
rejected_leads.reason: Spot checks showed real signature computation/verification (Signature.verify, MAC compare); no obvious bypass in the inspected code.
Error summaries are HTML-escaped before being placed in the SpEL template, and message converters do not render the exception type as HTML for text/html Accept; no injection identified there.

summary: Reviewed the spring-security-oauth source snapshot (parent version 2.0.10.BUILD-SNAPSHOT) across 445 files. The strongest source-supported issue is in the default OAuth2 whitelabel approval page: attacker-influenced `scope` values are concatenated unescaped into an HTML template that `SpelView` subsequently re-parses and evaluates with a permissive `StandardEvaluationContext`. This yields reflected HTML/JS injection and expression (SpEL) injection in the approval flow, with a configuration-dependent gate (client scope validation) and an ApprovalStore-based handler needed to populate the `scopes` model map. Other plausible leads (redirect-URI matching in DefaultRedirectResolver, JWT converter key handling, JDBC/Redis serialization, grant-type checks) were considered and are listed as rejected/unconfirmed, not as additional candidates. No runtime or test confirmation was possible because the snapshot contains main sources only (no test sources) and tools are read-only.
